primary_claim: Frontier AI models (Claude 3.5/3.7, GPT-4.5, GPT-4o, O1-Pro, Gemini 2.5 Pro) consistently fail to produce a correct machining plan for a simple manufacturing part, showing poor visual perception (with Gemini 2.5 Pro making partial progress) and persistent physical-reasoning errors even when the visual interpretation is accurate.

effect.metric: fraction of attempts with mostly-accurate visual feature identification (Gemini 2.5 Pro, the best-performing model)
effect.value: ~1 in 4 attempts identifies most major features without major hallucination; still always misses subtle details like corner radii, and physical-reasoning plans remain filled with practical errors

contradicts_or_qualifies: Dario Amodei's prediction that AI will lead to near-total simultaneous automation across jobs, putting workers 'in the same boat' — the author's case study suggests physical-world jobs will remain largely unaffected while white-collar automation proceeds
models' strong performance on visual reasoning benchmarks like MMMU, which the author argues doesn't correlate with real-world manufacturing usefulness
stated_future_work: explore synthetic data generated via simulation (e.g. CAM software for CNC machining) to address the lack of physical-task training data, though a simulation-reality gap and many processes lacking good simulators remain issues
limitations_stated: this evaluation only scratches the surface of the job — real machining requires managing many further details (tool clearance, rigidity trade-offs, etc.) that are inherently spatial and impossible to fully evaluate via text
for models other than Gemini 2.5 Pro it is hard to separate visual misunderstanding from deeper physical-reasoning errors, since poor vision confounds the plans
single case study of one relatively simple part and one manufacturing process (CNC machining)
quote: all models tested continue to fail significantly on physical reasoning. They still perform terribly overall.
